title_en: Round and Round: The Water Cycle
description_ru: Мы следуем за каплей воды по кругу: море, облако, снег, река и снова море. Так объясняется круговорот воды в природе.
text:
Imagine that you are a drop of water, and your name is Dot. You live in a warm, blue sea near the equator. You are very small, but you are part of something enormous, because the water of the Earth never stays in one place. It moves in a circle that has no beginning and no end. Scientists call this circle the water cycle. Let us follow Dot on her long journey.

One sunny morning, the sun heats the surface of the sea. Dot becomes warmer and warmer, and she moves faster and faster. Suddenly, she leaves the sea and rises into the air as an invisible gas called water vapour. This process is called evaporation. The sun is the engine of the whole cycle, and every day it lifts millions of tonnes of water from oceans, lakes and rivers. Plants help too, because they lose water through their leaves, and this is called transpiration.

As Dot rises, the air around her gets colder. At a height of two or three kilometres, the temperature is much lower than on the ground. Dot cools down, and she slows down. She meets millions of other drops of water vapour, and together they become tiny drops of liquid water. This is called condensation. Each drop attaches itself to a small piece of dust. Together, they make a cloud. A big cloud may contain more than a million kilograms of water, and it floats because the drops are so light.

The wind carries Dot's cloud over the sea and then over land. It reaches a high mountain, and the air is pushed upward. The cloud becomes colder, and the drops become bigger. They stick together and grow heavier and heavier. At some point, they are too heavy to float, and they fall. This is precipitation. If the air is very cold, Dot becomes a snowflake. If it is warmer, she falls as rain. Today it is cold, and Dot lands on the top of the mountain as snow.

For three months, Dot sleeps in a thick layer of snow. When spring arrives, the sun warms the mountain, and the snow begins to melt. Dot turns into liquid again and runs down the slope as a small stream. She joins other streams, and together they form a river. This is called runoff. Some of the water does not stay on the surface, though. A part of it goes down into the soil and moves slowly through the rocks. This water is called groundwater, and it can stay underground for years or even for thousands of years.

Dot is lucky, because she stays in the river. On her way to the sea, she passes a village, a forest and a farm. A farmer takes her to water his vegetables, and for some time, she is part of a tomato. Later, a person eats the tomato and drinks a glass of water too. Everything that lives needs water, and most of your body is made of it, about sixty percent in an adult. Water that you drink today may be very old, because the Earth always uses the same water again and again.

After several weeks, Dot is back in the river, and finally she reaches the ocean. There, in the warm sea, she is going to wait for another sunny morning. The cycle begins again. Some scientists say that a drop of water spends about nine days in the air, but thousands of years in the deep ocean, and even longer in the ice of the polar regions.

Dot also has relatives in the sky. Some of her friends fall as rain over a desert, where the ground is hot and dry, and they evaporate again before they touch the sand. Others land on a city, run into a drain and travel to a river through a pipe. Every drop has a different road, but the engine is always the same, the heat of the sun and the pull of gravity.

The water cycle is very important for people. It makes rain for our crops, keeps the weather stable, fills our rivers and gives us fresh drinking water. But only about three percent of the water on Earth is fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers. That is why we must use it carefully. When you turn off the tap while you brush your teeth, you help to protect the cycle. And somewhere in the world, a small drop called Dot continues her journey, and she will never stop.

questions.answer: Water vapour cools and turns into tiny drops around dust.

questions.answer: Rain or snow falling from the clouds.
